title: Manage Expectations to Improve Pre-Observation Conversations https://www.ollielovell.com/tot/141-manage-expectations-to-improve-pre-observation-conversations/
author: Lovell, Ollie
summary: Ollie Lovell argues that a coach's real leverage over whether feedback lands well comes before the observed lesson even happens, in the pre-observation conversation, because how coachees receive feedback depends less on its content than on whether it matches what they expected. He grounds this in reward-prediction-error research from neuroscience, quoting Daniel Lieberman on how dopamine responds to the gap between expectation and outcome rather than to objective good news. From there he offers three concrete scripts a coach can use before observing a lesson: naming upfront that the feedback will feel challenging, sharing a personal story of having once received similarly challenging feedback, and showing a video of what rehearsal will actually look like. Each script is paired with an explanation of the psychological mechanism it activates, from reframing challenge as evidence of progress to normalizing rehearsal as something even senior staff still do. Lovell frames all of this as applicable beyond formal coaching relationships, to any teacher trying to set a colleague's or a class's expectations before difficult feedback.
points: Lovell's central claim is that pre-observation framing, not the tone of the feedback itself, determines whether a coachee experiences feedback as fair or as an ambush.
He roots the argument in reward-prediction-error theory, using Daniel Lieberman's framing of dopamine as a response to the gap between expectation and outcome, not to objectively good news.
His "it wasn't until I received challenging feedback myself that I really improved" script works by positioning the coach's own past struggle as a model, not a lecture.
The rehearsal-video technique is designed to remove ambiguity about what a coaching session will actually feel like, which Lovell argues builds buy-in before it even starts.
quotes: We constantly make predictions about what’s coming next, from what time we can leave work, to how much money we expect to find when we check our balance at the ATM.

This is why, in coaching, pre-observation conversations are crucial. It’s isn’t so much how positive, negative, direct or facilitative the messaging is that influences how a coachee takes their feedback.
It sets the expectation that challenge will occur, and it reframes that challenge as meaning that progress is being made, rather than something that’s solely negative.
Rehearsal helps teachers to break unproductive old habits, and to form more productive new ones! But rehearsal is often foreign to coachees.

Showing a video of rehearsal makes it crystal clear to a coachee what that rehearsal will look like. That it’ll be hard work, that I’ll be explicit with my feedback and guidance, but also that we can have a bit of fun with it.
